title: A time for everything (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
hookLine: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to weep and to laugh

lines: THEN, IN CHAPTER THREE, A LIST.
cards: Vanity of vanities, the book begins, and all is vanity. The writer gives himself a title, Qoheleth in Hebrew, and in the first two chapters he tries everything: building, gardens, pleasure, wealth, wisdom.
Each time he comes back to the same word, hevel, a breath, a vapor, smoke that's gone when you reach for it. The Douay renders it vanity. Then, in chapter three, he stops arguing and writes a list.
A folk song once borrowed most of its lines, but they were here first.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven." Then fourteen pairs, each a time to do something and a time to do its opposite. A time to be born and a time to die.
A time to plant and a time to pull up. A time to weep and a time to laugh. A time to mourn and a time to dance.
A time to embrace and a time to keep away from embraces. A time to keep silence and a time to speak. A time of war and a time of peace.
Twenty-eight times, a whole life in pairs.

teach.h: NOT A TO-DO LIST: A DESCRIPTION.
teach.b: It's not a to-do list. Nobody chooses a time to die, or a time of war. It's a description: life comes in seasons, and you're always standing in one.
The Hebrew word for time, et, means the fitting moment.
A few verses later the writer says God has made all things good in their time, and has handed the world over to human minds to ponder; the Hebrew can also be read as eternity set in the heart.
Yet nobody can find out the whole work of God from beginning to end. People feel the bigger shape, but only ever see their own season of it.
The name Qoheleth is puzzling; it seems to mean one who gathers an assembly. The Greek translated it Ecclesiastes, from ekklesia, assembly, the same word that later meant church.
It's one of the readings a family may choose for a Catholic funeral. It doesn't rush grief.

teach.h: A TIME TO WEEP, AND A TIME TO LAUGH.
teach.b: It just says: this, too, has its time.

how: Ecclesiastes 3 is among the Old Testament readings Catholic families may choose for a funeral, and it is also read at weekday Mass.

a season of the farming year, like harvest
forever, the time that never ends

games.q: you're Qoheleth, writing about life under the sun. you've seen birth, death, war, dancing and grief. how do you describe it?
o: as a list of rules to follow.
as seasons: a time for every one of them.
as a mess with no shape at all.
games.why: "all things have their season." fourteen pairs, each with its time, and God, he says, has made everything good in its time.

practice: Go through a few of the pairs slowly and see which fits right now: a time to plant or to pull up, to keep silence or to speak, to mourn, or maybe to dance. Just name it, without judging, the way you'd say it's autumn.
If you pray, offer God the season you're in, and ask to live it well.

wordCard.voice: et. Hebrew for time, the fitting moment, repeating through Ecclesiastes' list of fourteen pairs: every season of a life has its moment under heaven. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: time, the fitting moment. it's the word that repeats through every line of the list.

carryVoice: Your line: a time for every purpose. Fourteen pairs, one whole life. That's day four hundred thirty-three.
